characters.name: Amos
characters.perkNote: Represents Amos's two successful intercessions in the vision cycle (7:1-6), where pleading with God directly turned aside coming judgment before it fell.

genealogy.note: No family lineage is given anywhere in the text — unusual for a writing prophet (contrast Hosea 1:1, 'son of Beeri,' or Joel 1:1, 'son of Pethuel'). Amos identifies himself only by trade and hometown: a herdman among the herdmen of Tekoa, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit (1:1; 7:14).

funFacts: Only Old Testament prophet explicitly identified as a herdman/sheep-breeder and a gatherer of sycomore fruit rather than a trained prophet or priest's son (7:14) — a point he makes himself, directly to a hostile priest, as proof his call came from God and not from prophetic guild training.
From Tekoa in the southern kingdom of Judah, but sent north to prophesy against Israel, centered on the royal sanctuary at Bethel — a foreign critic in the eyes of his audience.
His prophetic ministry is dated to 'two years before the earthquake' (1:1), a quake evidently severe enough to still be remembered generations later (cf. Zechariah 14:5).

Twice personally interceded with God in the vision cycle and saw judgment averted (7:1-6) — 'the LORD repented for this: It shall not be' — before the visions shift to unaverted, final judgment (see the Visions of Judgment entry).

verses.note: Superscription: 'The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa... in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.' Naming note: 'Uzziah' is the same king called 'Azariah' through most of 2 Kings (e.g. 2 Kings 15:1-7) — KJV itself uses both names for one man, not two kings. Naming collision flag: 'Jeroboam the son of Joash' is Jeroboam II, distinct from the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat (1 Kings 11-14) who founded Israel's rival worship system — both are called simply 'Jeroboam' elsewhere in Kings/Chronicles.

Opening theophany: 'The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither' — sets the book's tone before the nation-by-nation oracles begin.

Amos personally intercedes twice in the vision cycle and both times judgment is averted as a direct result. First, shown a vision of grasshoppers devouring the land's latter growth, he pleads, 'O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small' — 'The LORD repented for this: It shall not be, saith the LORD' (7:1-3). Second, shown a vision of judgment by fire devouring 'the great deep,' he pleads again, 'O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small' — 'The LORD repented for this: This also shall not be, saith the Lord GOD' (7:4-6). His most personally embodied, dialogic exchange with God in the book.

Answering Amaziah: 'I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.'

Amos pronounces personal judgment on Amaziah in direct response to being told to stop prophesying: 'Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thy land shall be divided by line... and Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land.' Naming note: Amos quotes Amaziah's own words back, 'drop not thy word against the house of Isaac' — 'Isaac' here is a poetic synonym for the nation of Israel, not a fresh appearance of the patriarch Isaac of Genesis.

characters.name: Amaziah
characters.perkNote: Represents the priestly establishment's attempt to shut down Amos's prophecy at Bethel — answered directly by a personal judgment oracle naming his own household (7:16-17).

genealogy.note: No individual family members are named. Amos's judgment oracle against Amaziah (7:17) mentions an unnamed wife ('thy wife shall be an harlot in the city') and unnamed sons and daughters ('thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword'), but none are given personal names in the text.

funFacts: Priest of Bethel — Israel's royal sanctuary, not Jerusalem's temple — making him a state religious official, not an independent figure (7:10).
The only person in the book of Amos who directly confronts the prophet and is directly, personally answered with a named judgment oracle in return (7:16-17).
Calls Amos 'thou seer' (7:12) — a term for a prophet — while simultaneously ordering him to leave Israel, an implicit acknowledgment of Amos's prophetic status even while trying to silence him.

verses.note: Amaziah reports Amos to the king: 'Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land.' Naming collision flag: this 'Jeroboam' is Jeroboam II (son of Joash, 1:1), not the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat of 1 Kings — both share the bare name 'Jeroboam' elsewhere in the Deuteronomistic history.

Amaziah confronts Amos directly: 'O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.'

Amos quotes Amaziah's demand back to him before pronouncing judgment: 'Thou sayest, Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac.' Naming note: 'house of Isaac' is a poetic name for Israel/the nation, not the patriarch Isaac of Genesis appearing in person — flagged to avoid confusion with the Genesis Isaac entry.

characters.name: Oracles Against the Nations
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, through Amos, opening the book (Amos 1:3-2:16)
characters.purpose: A rhetorical trap — Amos indicts Israel's neighbors and Judah one by one for their own well-known atrocities, letting a Judean/Israelite audience nod along in agreement, before the same 'for three transgressions...and for four' formula lands, unavoidably, on Israel itself (2:6-16) — the true target of the whole sequence.
funFacts: Uses an identical 'for three transgressions...and for four' refrain eight times running, so listeners are already agreeing with judgment on their enemies before the formula turns on them.

Israel's oracle (2:6-16) is by far the longest of the eight and the only one detailing specific covenant/social sins rather than war crimes against other nations — marking it as the real target of the whole sequence.

verses.note: Damascus/Syria: judged 'because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron'; fire sent into 'the house of Hazael,' devouring 'the palaces of Benhadad'; the bar of Damascus broken and the people carried captive to Kir.
Gaza/Philistia: judged 'because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom.'
Tyre: judged 'because they delivered up the whole captivity to Edom, and remembered not the brotherly covenant.'
Edom: judged 'because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever.'
Ammon: judged 'because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border.'
Moab: judged 'because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime.'
Judah: judged 'because they have despised the law of the LORD, and have not kept his commandments, and their lies caused them to err.'
Israel: judged 'because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes' — the longest and climactic oracle, the true target the earlier seven were building toward.

characters.name: Social Injustice & False Worship
characters.deliveredBy: Amos, prophesying against Israel and Samaria (Amos 3-6)
characters.purpose: Details exactly why judgment falls on Israel: exploitation of the poor, corrupt courts, luxury built on oppression, and empty ritual worship offered without justice — 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' (5:24) is the book's own summary of what is missing.
funFacts: 'Kine of Bashan' (4:1) is one of the most memorable insults in prophetic literature — comparing Samaria's wealthy women to the fattened cattle of Bashan's rich pastureland.
5:24's 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' is one of the most widely echoed single verses from any Minor Prophet in later usage and rhetoric.

verses.note: 'You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities' — election creates accountability, not exemption.
'Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan, that are in the mountain of Samaria, which oppress the poor, which crush the needy' — addressed to Samaria's wealthy women.
'Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel' — closing refrain of a chapter cataloguing disasters Israel ignored as warnings.
'They afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right' — corrupt courts named directly.
'Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD!... the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light' — the expected day of vindication reversed into a day of judgment.

'I hate, I despise your feast days... take thou away from me the noise of thy songs... but let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' — ritual worship rejected without justice behind it.
Those 'that lie upon beds of ivory... but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph' — luxury indicted for its indifference, not the luxury itself.

characters.name: Visions of Judgment
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, shown to Amos in three further visions (Amos 7:7-9; 8:1-3; 9:1-4)
characters.purpose: Where the first two visions of the cycle (grasshoppers, fire) were turned aside by Amos's intercession, these three are not — judgment moves from a warning that could still be averted to a sentence declared final and unappealable.
funFacts: The plumbline vision gives the book its most enduring image — Israel tested against a fixed, unmovable standard rather than a shifting one.
The Hebrew wordplay in the summer-fruit vision (qayits, 'summer fruit,' sounding like qets, 'the end') is lost in English translation but is the entire point of the vision (8:1-2).

verses.note: Plumbline vision: 'Behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand... Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more.' Naming note: 'the high places of Isaac' (7:9) is a poetic name for Israel, not the patriarch Isaac appearing in person. Naming collision flag: 'the house of Jeroboam' here refers to Jeroboam II (1:1), not Jeroboam I son of Nebat.
Basket of summer fruit vision: 'The end is come upon my people of Israel; I will not again pass by them any more.'

Within the same vision unit: indictment of dishonest trade — 'making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit... that we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes.'

Vision of the Lord standing beside the altar, commanding the posts struck so they shake: 'he that fleeth of them shall not flee away, and he that escapeth of them shall not be delivered' — no intercession is recorded in response to this vision, unlike the first two.

characters.name: Restoration of David's Fallen Booth
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, closing the book through Amos (Amos 9:11-15)
characters.purpose: After nine chapters of near-unrelieved judgment, the book ends on a sudden reversal — a promise to raise up the fallen tabernacle (booth) of David, rebuild ruined cities, and restore agricultural abundance, so the book that opened with the LORD roaring in judgment (1:2) closes with unconditional hope.
funFacts: Quoted directly by James at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15:16-17 as scriptural warrant for including Gentiles in the church — one of the most consequential New Testament citations of any Minor Prophet.

verses.note: 'In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old.' Naming note: 'David' here is a dynastic reference to the fallen Davidic line, not the person of David appearing on-page — flagged to avoid confusion with the David of Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Psalms.

'The plowman shall overtake the reaper... I will bring again the captivity of my people of Israel, and they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit them... and they shall no more be pulled up out of their land which I have given them, saith the LORD thy God.'

notes: Redraft addresses the single fact-check finding: Amos's own entry now cites Amos 7:1-6 (both intercessions — grasshoppers and fire — and their reversal), his most personally dialogic moment with God in the book. Structure: 2 person-tier managers (Amos; Amaziah, promoted from a background figure to a full manager per rule 3 since he has his own confrontation scene, quoted dialogue, and a personally-named judgment oracle against his household) and 4 law/theme tiers covering the book's major structural units (Oracles Against the Nations, ch.1-2; Social Injustice & False Worship, ch.3-6; Visions of Judgment — the three unaverted visions, distinct from the two averted ones covered under Amos himself; and Restoration of David's Fallen Booth, 9:11-15). No separate entries were created for Uzziah or Jeroboam (II) — neither speaks or acts on-page in Amos, appearing only as chronological/reported markers — but both are cited in Amos's and Amaziah's verse notes to satisfy the 'covered somewhere' rule. Naming collisions flagged every time they occur, not just once: Uzziah/Azariah (same king, two KJV names, per the Hizkiah/Hezekiah-style pattern); Jeroboam II (son of Joash) vs. the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat, flagged at both 1:1 and 7:9-11; 'house/high places of Isaac' (7:9, 7:16) as a poetic name for Israel rather than the patriarch, flagged at both occurrences; 'tabernacle of David' (9:11) as a dynastic reference rather than the person of David. KJV spelling preserved exactly, including 'sycomore' (not 'sycamore') and 'grasshoppers' (not 'locusts') in 7:1 — the latter specifically avoids the kind of invented-detail error flagged in the accuracy rules (KJV's own word choice, not a synonym).
